docs.title: Overview
docs.text: hya is a library of custom OmegaConf resolvers designed to be used with Hydra. It provides a comprehensive set of resolvers for mathematical operations, path manipulation, data type conversions, and more.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
The default resolvers are automatically registered when you import hya:

import hya
from omegaconf import OmegaConf

# Use resolvers in your configuration
conf = OmegaConf.create(
    {
        "batch_size": 32,
        "num_samples": 1000,
        "num_batches": "${hya.ceildiv:${num_samples},${batch_size}}",
        "learning_rate": "${hya.pow:10,-3}",  # 0.001
    }
)

print(conf.num_batches)  # Output: 32
print(conf.learning_rate)  # Output: 0.001

docs.title: Using with Hydra
docs.text:
Create a configuration file config.yaml:

model:
  input_dim: 784
  hidden_dim: 256
  output_dim: 10

training:
  batch_size: 32
  num_epochs: 10
  learning_rate: ${hya.pow:10,-3} # 0.001

paths:
  data_dir: ${hya.path:/data}
  model_dir: ${hya.iter_join:[${paths.data_dir},models,v1],/}

experiment:
  name: mnist_classifier
  id: ${hya.sha256:${experiment.name}}

Then use it in your Python script:

import hya
import hydra
from omegaconf import DictConfig


@hydra.main(version_base=None, config_path=".", config_name="config")
def main(cfg: DictConfig):
    print(f"Learning rate: {cfg.training.learning_rate}")
    print(f"Model dir: {cfg.paths.model_dir}")
    print(f"Experiment ID: {cfg.experiment.id}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Registering Custom Resolvers
docs.text:
You can extend hya with your own custom resolvers:

from hya import get_default_registry

registry = get_default_registry()


@registry.register("multiply")
def multiply_resolver(x, y):
    return x * y


# Register the custom resolver with OmegaConf
registry.register_resolvers()

# Now use it in your configuration
conf = OmegaConf.create({"result": "${multiply:5,3}"})
print(conf.result)  # Output: 15

docs.title: Available Resolvers
docs.text:
hya provides over 20 built-in resolvers organized into categories:

  • Mathematical operations: add, sub, mul, truediv, floordiv, ceildiv, pow, sqrt, neg, max, min, exp, log, log10, sinh, asinh
  • Constants: pi
  • Path utilities: path, iter_join
  • Utilities: len, sha256
  • Optional (with dependencies):
  • NumPy: np.array
  • PyTorch: torch.tensor, torch.dtype
  • Braceexpand: braceexpand

See the Resolvers page for complete documentation of all resolvers.

docs.title: API stability
docs.text: While hya is in development stage, no API is guaranteed to be stable from one release to the next. In fact, it is very likely that the API will change multiple times before a stable 1.0.0 release. In practice, this means that upgrading hya to a new version will possibly break any code that was using the old version of hya.

docs.title: Get Started
docs.text: It is highly recommended to install in a virtual environment to keep your system in order.

docs.title: Installing with uv (recommended)
docs.text:
The following command installs the latest version of the library:

uv pip install hya

To make the package as slim as possible, only the packages required to use hya are installed. This minimal installation includes only omegaconf, which is sufficient for using all the core resolvers.

docs.title: Installing Optional Dependencies
docs.text:
hya provides additional resolvers that require optional dependencies:

# Install all optional dependencies
uv pip install 'hya[all]'

# Install specific optional dependencies
uv pip install hya braceexpand  # For hya.braceexpand resolver
uv pip install hya numpy        # For hya.np.array resolver
uv pip install hya torch        # For hya.torch.tensor and hya.torch.dtype resolvers

docs.title: Dependency Matrix
docs.text:
The following table shows which resolvers require which packages:

Resolver Required Package Description hya.braceexpand braceexpand>=0.1.7 Brace expansion patterns hya.np.array numpy>=1.24 NumPy array creation hya.torch.tensor torch>=2.0 PyTorch tensor creation hya.torch.dtype torch>=2.0 PyTorch data type specification

All other resolvers work with the base installation (only omegaconf required).

If you try to use a resolver that requires an optional package without installing it, you'll receive a helpful error message indicating which package needs to be installed.

docs.title: Installing from source
docs.text:
To install hya from source, you can follow the steps below. First, you will need to install uv. uv is used to manage and install the dependencies. If uv is already installed on your machine, you can skip this step. You can check the uv installation by running the following command:

uv --version

Then, you can clone the git repository:

git clone git@github.com:durandtibo/hya.git

It is recommended to create a Python 3.11+ virtual environment. This step is optional so you can skip it. To create a virtual environment, you can use the following command:

make conda

It automatically creates a conda virtual environment. When the virtual environment is created, you can activate it with the following command:

conda activate hya

This example uses conda to create a virtual environment, but you can use other tools or configurations. Then, you should install the required package to use hya with the following command:

make install

This command will install all the required packages. You can also use this command to update the required packages. This command will check if there is a more recent package available and will install it. Finally, you can test the installation with the following command:

make unit-test-cov

docs.title: Resolvers
docs.text: This page provides comprehensive documentation for all resolvers implemented in hya.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
hya provides over 20 built-in resolvers for use in OmegaConf/Hydra configurations. Resolvers are organized into the following categories:

  • Arithmetic Operations: Basic mathematical operations (add, subtract, multiply, divide)
  • Advanced Math: Transcendental and special functions (exp, log, sqrt, powers)
  • Comparison: Min/max operations
  • Path Utilities: Path creation and manipulation
  • String Utilities: Joining and hashing
  • Utility Functions: Length, negation, constants
  • Optional Resolvers: Require additional packages (NumPy, PyTorch, braceexpand)

All resolvers are automatically available after importing hya.

docs.title: Default Resolvers
docs.text: These resolvers are available with the base installation (no optional dependencies required).

docs.title: Standard Library Resolvers
docs.text:
These resolvers are registered as the standard library callable itself, with no wrapper: the behaviour, the accepted arguments and the error messages are the ones of the callable. See the documentation of the callable for the details.

Key Callable Example Result hya.sub operator.sub ${hya.sub:100,30} 70 hya.truediv operator.truediv ${hya.truediv:10,4} 2.5 hya.floordiv operator.floordiv ${hya.floordiv:100,32} 3 hya.neg operator.neg ${hya.neg:5} -5 hya.pow operator.pow ${hya.pow:10,-3} 0.001 hya.sqrt math.sqrt ${hya.sqrt:64} 8.0 hya.exp math.exp ${hya.exp:0} 1.0 hya.log math.log ${hya.log:8,2} 3.0 hya.log10 math.log10 ${hya.log10:1000} 3.0 hya.sinh math.sinh ${hya.sinh:0} 0.0 hya.asinh math.asinh ${hya.asinh:0} 0.0 hya.max max ${hya.max:10,25,15} 25 hya.min min ${hya.min:10,25,15} 10 hya.len len ${hya.len:[1,2,3]} 3

Examples with interpolations:

dataset:
  total_samples: 60000
  val_samples: 10000
  train_samples: ${hya.sub:${dataset.total_samples},${dataset.val_samples}} # 50000
  warmup_ratio: ${hya.truediv:1000,${dataset.total_samples}} # 0.016666...

model:
  embedding_dim: 512
  head_dim: ${hya.floordiv:${model.embedding_dim},8} # 64
  scale_factor: ${hya.sqrt:${model.embedding_dim}} # 22.627...
  layer_sizes: [128, 256, 512, 1024]
  num_layers: ${hya.len:${model.layer_sizes}} # 4
  actual_layers: ${hya.max:${model.num_layers},8} # 8

docs.title: hya.add
docs.text:
Adds multiple values together.

Syntax: ${hya.add:value1,value2,...}

Example:

# Simple addition
total: ${hya.add:10,20} # Result: 30

# Multiple values
sum: ${hya.add:1,2,3,4,5} # Result: 15

# With references
training:
  train_samples: 50000
  val_samples: 10000
  total_samples: ${hya.add:${training.train_samples},${training.val_samples}} # Result: 60000

Equivalent Python:

value = value1 + value2 + value3 + ...

Note: The arguments are never modified: ${hya.add:${x},[3]} returns a new list and leaves x unchanged. At least one argument is required.

docs.title: hya.mul
docs.text:
Multiplies multiple values together.

Syntax: ${hya.mul:value1,value2,...}

Example:

# Simple multiplication
area: ${hya.mul:10,20} # Result: 200

# Multiple values
volume: ${hya.mul:5,10,2} # Result: 100

# Compute total parameters
model:
  layers: 12
  hidden_size: 768
  total_params: ${hya.mul:${model.layers},${model.hidden_size}} # Result: 9216

Equivalent Python:

value = object1 * object2 * object3 * ...

Note: The arguments are never modified and are meant to be numbers. Repeating a list of the configuration (${hya.mul:${x},2} with x: [1, 2]) is not supported and raises an error. At least one argument is required.

docs.title: hya.ceildiv
docs.text:
Performs ceiling division (rounds up to nearest integer).

Syntax: ${hya.ceildiv:dividend,divisor}

Example:

batches: ${hya.ceildiv:100,32} # Result: 4

# Calculate number of batches needed
training:
  samples: 10000
  batch_size: 64
  num_batches: ${hya.ceildiv:${training.samples},${training.batch_size}} # Result: 157

Equivalent Python:

value = -(dividend // -divisor)  # Canonical implementation (no floating point)
# Alternative (but may have precision issues with large integers):
# value = math.ceil(dividend / divisor)

Use Case: Calculating the number of batches needed to process all samples.

docs.title: hya.pi
docs.text:
Returns the mathematical constant π (pi).

Syntax: ${hya.pi:}

Example:

pi_value: ${hya.pi:} # Result: 3.14159...

geometry:
  radius: 5
  circumference: ${hya.mul:2,${hya.pi:},${geometry.radius}} # Result: 31.41...

Equivalent Python:

import math

value = math.pi

docs.title: hya.path
docs.text:
Converts a string, or a file: URL, to a resolved pathlib.Path object with user expansion.

Syntax: ${hya.path:path_string}

Example:

data_dir: ${hya.path:/data/datasets}
model_path: ${hya.path:"~/models/checkpoint.pth"}
local_file: ${hya.path:file:///data/file.txt}
url_decoded: ${hya.path:file:///data/my%20file.txt} # /data/my file.txt

Equivalent Python:

from pathlib import Path
from urllib.parse import unquote, urlparse

if path.startswith("file:"):
    path = unquote(urlparse(path).path)
value = Path(path).expanduser().resolve()

Notes:

  • Returns a pathlib.Path object, which is useful for path operations in Python.
  • Only a string that starts with file: is read as a URL (its percent-encoding is decoded and its query is dropped). Any other string is a plain path, written as is: /data/a?b and /data/a%20b keep the ? and the %20.
  • A path with a tilde must be quoted in an interpolation: ${hya.path:"~/data"}. Unquoted, it is a grammar error.
  • hya.to_path was merged into hya.path in 0.5.0.

docs.title: hya.iter_join
docs.text:
Joins elements of an iterable into a string with a separator.

Syntax: ${hya.iter_join:iterable,separator}

Example:

# Simple join
joined: ${hya.iter_join:[a,b,c],-} # Result: "a-b-c"

# Build paths
paths:
  root: data
  project: myproject
  version: v1
  full_path: ${hya.iter_join:[${paths.root},${paths.project},${paths.version}],/}
  # Result: "data/myproject/v1"

# Build experiment names
experiment:
  model: resnet
  dataset: cifar10
  name: ${hya.iter_join:[${experiment.model},${experiment.dataset}],_}
  # Result: "resnet_cifar10"

Equivalent Python:

value = separator.join(map(str, iterable))

Use Case: Dynamically constructing file paths, experiment names, or configuration strings.

docs.title: hya.sha256
docs.text:
Computes the SHA-256 hash of an object.

Syntax: ${hya.sha256:object}

Example:

hash: ${hya.sha256:mystring}
# Result: "bd3ff47540b31e62d4ca6b07794e5a886b0f655fc322730f26ecd65cc7dd5c90"

experiment:
  config: "resnet50_adam_0.001"
  version_id: ${hya.sha256:${experiment.config}}
  # Generates consistent hash for versioning

Equivalent Python:

import hashlib

value = hashlib.sha256(bytes(str(obj), "utf-8")).hexdigest()

Use Case: Creating unique identifiers for experiments, cache keys, or version tracking.

docs.title: Optional Resolvers
docs.text: These resolvers require additional packages to be installed.

docs.title: Braceexpand
docs.text:
Package Required: braceexpand>=0.1.7

Install with: pip install braceexpand

docs.title: hya.braceexpand
docs.text:
Expands brace patterns similar to bash brace expansion.

Syntax: ${hya.braceexpand:pattern}

Example:

# Numeric range
files: ${hya.braceexpand:"file_{1..5}.txt"}
# Returns a list: [file_1.txt, file_2.txt, ..., file_5.txt]

# Choice expansion
configs: ${hya.braceexpand:"config_{train,val,test}.yaml"}
# Returns a list: [config_train.yaml, config_val.yaml, config_test.yaml]

# Nested patterns
paths: ${hya.braceexpand:"data/{2020..2022}/{jan,feb,mar}"}
# Returns a list: [data/2020/jan, data/2020/feb, ..., data/2022/mar]

# The list can be used by another resolver
names: ${hya.iter_join:${hya.braceexpand:"a{1..3}"},-} # Result: "a1-a2-a3"

Notes:

  • The pattern must be quoted (or its braces escaped) in an interpolation: unquoted, the braces are a grammar error of OmegaConf.
  • The resolver returns a list, not an iterator: it has a length, can be indexed and can be read several times. The whole expansion is built at once.

Reference: braceexpand documentation

docs.title: NumPy
docs.text:
Package Required: numpy>=1.24

Install with: pip install numpy

docs.title: hya.np.array
docs.text:
Converts data to a NumPy array.

Syntax: ${hya.np.array:data}

Example:

# 1D array
vector: ${hya.np.array:[1,2,3,4,5]}

# 2D array
matrix: ${hya.np.array:[[1,2,3],[4,5,6]]}

# Use in configuration
data:
  shape: [28, 28]
  default_image: ${hya.np.array:${data.shape}}

Equivalent Python:

import numpy as np

value = np.array(data)

docs.title: PyTorch
docs.text:
Package Required: torch>=2.0

Install with: pip install torch

docs.title: hya.torch.tensor
docs.text:
Converts data to a PyTorch tensor.

Syntax: ${hya.torch.tensor:data}

Example:

# 1D tensor
weights: ${hya.torch.tensor:[0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4]}

# 2D tensor
matrix: ${hya.torch.tensor:[[1,2],[3,4]]}

# Use in model configuration
model:
  default_bias: ${hya.torch.tensor:[0.0,0.0,0.0]}

Equivalent Python:

import torch

value = torch.tensor(data)

docs.title: hya.torch.dtype
docs.text:
Creates a PyTorch dtype from its string representation.

Syntax: ${hya.torch.dtype:dtype_name}

Example:

# Common dtypes
float_type: ${hya.torch.dtype:float32}
int_type: ${hya.torch.dtype:int64}
bool_type: ${hya.torch.dtype:bool}

# Use in model configuration
model:
  compute_dtype: ${hya.torch.dtype:float16}
  parameter_dtype: ${hya.torch.dtype:float32}

training:
  use_mixed_precision: true
  amp_dtype: ${hya.torch.dtype:float16}

Available dtypes: Common dtype string names include float, float16, float32, float64, bfloat16, int, int8, int16, int32, int64, uint8, bool, complex64, complex128. The exact available dtypes depend on your PyTorch installation. For a complete list, see the PyTorch dtype documentation.

Equivalent Python:

import torch

value = torch.float32  # for dtype_name="float32"

Note: An unknown name raises an InterpolationResolutionError whose message lists the available dtype names, sorted.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text: This guide provides comprehensive information on using hya in your projects.

docs.title: Importing and Automatic Registration
docs.text:
When you import hya, all default resolvers are automatically registered with OmegaConf:

import hya
from omegaconf import OmegaConf

# Resolvers are now available
conf = OmegaConf.create({"result": "${hya.add:2,3}"})
print(conf.result)  # Output: 5

The optional resolvers (hya.braceexpand, hya.np.array, hya.torch.tensor, hya.torch.dtype) are registered only if their package is installed. import hya does not import numpy, torch or braceexpand: the module of an optional resolver is imported on the first call of that resolver.

docs.title: Using Resolvers in YAML Configurations
docs.text:
You can use resolvers directly in YAML configuration files:

# config.yaml
model:
  layers: 4
  hidden_size: 256
  # NOTE: This is a simple demonstration of the mul resolver
  # Real neural network parameter counts are much more complex
  approx_params: ${hya.mul:${model.layers},${model.hidden_size}}

training:
  total_samples: 10000
  batch_size: 32
  num_batches: ${hya.ceildiv:${training.total_samples},${training.batch_size}}
  learning_rate: ${hya.pow:10,-3} # 10^-3 = 0.001

Load and use the configuration:

import hya
from omegaconf import OmegaConf

conf = OmegaConf.load("config.yaml")
print(conf.model.approx_params)  # Output: 1024
print(conf.training.num_batches)  # Output: 313
print(conf.training.learning_rate)  # Output: 0.001

docs.title: Integration with Hydra
docs.text: hya is designed to work seamlessly with Hydra.

docs.title: Basic Hydra Example
docs.text:
config.yaml:

dataset:
  name: mnist
  train_samples: 60000
  val_samples: 10000
  total_samples: ${hya.add:${dataset.train_samples},${dataset.val_samples}}

model:
  type: cnn
  channels: [32, 64, 128]
  num_layers: ${hya.len:${model.channels}}

training:
  batch_size: 64
  epochs: 10
  steps_per_epoch: ${hya.ceildiv:${dataset.train_samples},${training.batch_size}}

paths:
  root: /data
  train: ${hya.iter_join:[${paths.root},${dataset.name},train],/}
  val: ${hya.iter_join:[${paths.root},${dataset.name},val],/}

experiment:
  name: ${dataset.name}_${model.type}
  version: ${hya.sha256:${experiment.name}}

train.py:

import hya
import hydra
from omegaconf import DictConfig


@hydra.main(version_base=None, config_path=".", config_name="config")
def train(cfg: DictConfig):
    print(f"Dataset: {cfg.dataset.name}")
    print(f"Total samples: {cfg.dataset.total_samples}")
    print(f"Model layers: {cfg.model.num_layers}")
    print(f"Steps per epoch: {cfg.training.steps_per_epoch}")
    print(f"Train path: {cfg.paths.train}")
    print(f"Experiment version: {cfg.experiment.version}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    train()

docs.title: Multi-Config with Hydra
docs.text:
You can use hya resolvers across multiple configuration files:

config.yaml:

defaults:
  - model: resnet
  - optimizer: adam

experiment:
  name: ${model.name}_${optimizer.name}
  seed: 42
  version: ${hya.sha256:${experiment.name}_${experiment.seed}}

model/resnet.yaml:

name: resnet
depth: 50
width_multiplier: 1.0
effective_depth: ${hya.mul:${model.depth},${model.width_multiplier}}

optimizer/adam.yaml:

name: adam
lr: ${hya.pow:10,-4} # 0.0001
betas: [0.9, 0.999]

docs.title: Creating and Registering Custom Resolvers
docs.text:
You can extend hya with your own custom resolvers:

from hya import get_default_registry

# Get the default registry
registry = get_default_registry()


# Register a simple custom resolver
@registry.register("double")
def double_resolver(x):
    """Double the input value."""
    return x * 2


# Register a more complex resolver
@registry.register("clip")
def clip_resolver(value, min_val, max_val):
    """Clip a value between min and max."""
    return max(min_val, min(value, max_val))


# Register custom resolvers with OmegaConf
# Note: Default hya resolvers are already registered on import
# This only registers your custom resolvers added to the default registry
registry.register_resolvers()

Now use them in your configuration:

hyperparameters:
  base_lr: 0.001
  scaled_lr: ${double:${hyperparameters.base_lr}}

  dropout: 0.7
  clipped_dropout: ${clip:${hyperparameters.dropout},0.0,0.5}

docs.title: Overriding Existing Resolvers
docs.text:
You can override a resolver of the registry with the keyword-only exist_ok parameter. The default resolvers are already published to OmegaConf when hya is imported, so register_resolvers() does not replace them silently: it skips the key and emits a warning. Use replace=True to replace the resolver of OmegaConf:

from hya import get_default_registry

registry = get_default_registry()


@registry.register("hya.add", exist_ok=True)
def custom_add(first, *others):
    """Custom add that also prints the result."""
    result = first + sum(others)
    print(f"Adding {(first, *others)} = {result}")
    return result


# Without replace=True, the old resolver is kept and a warning is emitted
registry.register_resolvers(replace=True)

register_resolvers is idempotent: calling it twice changes nothing, and a resolver that is already published is not registered again. A key that another source registered in OmegaConf is not overwritten unless replace=True.

OmegaConf caches the value of the nodes it has already resolved. Replacing a resolver does not clear this cache for existing configurations: call OmegaConf.clear_cache(cfg) to clear it.

The resolvers are published with annotation_validation="off": the type annotations of a resolver are documentation for readers and type checkers, OmegaConf does not check them at call time.

docs.title: Registering a Resolver Lazily
docs.text:
register_lazy registers a resolver as a "module:function" string. The module is imported the first time OmegaConf calls the resolver, not when the resolver is registered. This is how hya registers the resolvers that need a heavy optional package:

from hya import get_default_registry

registry = get_default_registry()
registry.register_lazy("my.array", "hya.numpy:to_array_resolver")
registry.register_resolvers()

A target that is not formatted as "module:function" raises a ValueError when it is registered. An unknown module or function raises an error on the first call of the resolver.

docs.title: Creating Isolated Registries
docs.text:
For advanced use cases, you can create independent registries:

from hya.registry import ResolverRegistry

# Create a new, isolated registry
custom_registry = ResolverRegistry()


@custom_registry.register("custom.multiply")
def multiply(x, y):
    return x * y


# Register only these custom resolvers
custom_registry.register_resolvers()

ResolverRegistry is also available from the top-level package: from hya import ResolverRegistry.

docs.title: Path Construction
docs.text:
Build file paths dynamically:

paths:
  root: /data
  project: myproject
  version: v1

  # Build paths using iter_join
  data_dir: ${hya.iter_join:[${paths.root},${paths.project},${paths.version}],/}
  train_file: ${hya.iter_join:[${paths.data_dir},train.csv],/}

  # Use path resolver for proper Path objects
  model_checkpoint: ${hya.path:${paths.data_dir}/models/checkpoint.pth}

  # A tilde must be quoted in an interpolation (unquoted, it is a grammar error)
  home_dir: ${hya.path:"~/data"}

docs.title: Mathematical Computations
docs.text:
Perform calculations in your configuration:

model:
  embedding_dim: 512
  num_heads: 8
  head_dim: ${hya.floordiv:${model.embedding_dim},${model.num_heads}} # 64

training:
  total_steps: 100000
  warmup_ratio: 0.1
  # 100000 * 0.1 is the float 10000.0: use ceildiv to get an integer
  warmup_steps: ${hya.ceildiv:${training.total_steps},10} # 10000

  # Calculate batch size for distributed training
  per_device_batch_size: 16
  num_devices: 4
  global_batch_size: ${hya.mul:${training.per_device_batch_size},${training.num_devices}}

docs.title: Data Type Specifications (PyTorch)
docs.text:
Specify tensor data types in configuration:

model:
  dtype: ${hya.torch.dtype:float32}
  use_half_precision: false
  compute_dtype: ${hya.torch.dtype:float16}

data:
  input_shape: [3, 224, 224]
  dummy_input: ${hya.torch.tensor:${data.input_shape}}

docs.title: Versioning and Hashing
docs.text:
Generate consistent identifiers:

experiment:
  model_name: resnet50
  dataset: imagenet
  augmentation: heavy

  # Create a unique experiment ID
  full_name: ${experiment.model_name}_${experiment.dataset}_${experiment.augmentation}
  experiment_id: ${hya.sha256:${experiment.full_name}}

  # Use for reproducible paths
  output_dir: ${hya.iter_join:[outputs,${experiment.experiment_id}],/}

docs.title: List Operations
docs.text:
Work with lists and sequences:

datasets:
  train: [mnist, cifar10, imagenet]
  num_datasets: ${hya.len:${datasets.train}}

  # Join dataset names
  combined_name: ${hya.iter_join:${datasets.train},_} # mnist_cifar10_imagenet

docs.title: Brace Expansion (requires braceexpand)
docs.text:
Generate multiple values from patterns:

files:
  # Expands to a list: file_1.txt, file_2.txt, ..., file_5.txt
  pattern: ${hya.braceexpand:"file_{1..5}.txt"}

  # Expands to a list: train_a.json, train_b.json, train_c.json
  train_configs: ${hya.braceexpand:"train_{a,b,c}.json"}

The pattern must be quoted in an interpolation. The result is a list (it has a length, can be indexed and can be read several times), so it can be used by other resolvers such as hya.iter_join.

docs.title: Checking for Resolvers
docs.text:
Check if a resolver is registered:

from hya import get_default_registry

registry = get_default_registry()

# Check if a resolver exists
if registry.has_resolver("hya.add"):
    print("add resolver is available")

# List all registered resolvers
for key in registry.state.keys():
    print(f"Registered: {key}")

docs.title: Accessing Registry State
docs.text:
from hya import get_default_registry

registry = get_default_registry()

# Get all registered resolvers: a read-only mapping (use registry.register to add one)
resolvers_dict = registry.state

# Count resolvers
print(f"Total resolvers: {len(resolvers_dict)}")

# Check specific resolvers
core_resolvers = [k for k in resolvers_dict.keys() if k.startswith("hya.")]
print(f"Core hya resolvers: {len(core_resolvers)}")

docs.title: Configuration Organization
docs.text:
Organize your configurations for maintainability:

# Good: Use resolvers to avoid duplication
model:
  hidden_size: 768
  num_layers: 12
  total_hidden: ${hya.mul:${model.hidden_size},${model.num_layers}}

# Avoid: Hardcoding computed values
# total_hidden: 9216  # If you change hidden_size, this becomes incorrect

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
An optional resolver is registered only when its package is installed. When the package is missing, the key is unknown to OmegaConf and the access raises UnsupportedInterpolationType. An error raised by a resolver is reported by OmegaConf as an InterpolationResolutionError:

import hya
from omegaconf import OmegaConf, errors

try:
    conf = OmegaConf.create({"tensor": "${hya.torch.tensor:[1,2,3]}"})
    print(conf.tensor)
except errors.UnsupportedInterpolationType:
    print("Error: PyTorch is required. Install with: pip install torch")

docs.title: Type Safety
docs.text:
Use appropriate resolvers for type safety:

# Good: Use correct division operators
samples: 1000
batch_size: 32
num_batches: ${hya.ceildiv:${samples},${batch_size}} # Integer result: 32

# Avoid: Using wrong division type
# num_batches: ${hya.truediv:${samples},${batch_size}}  # Float result: 31.25

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
Resolvers are evaluated lazily when accessed:

conf = OmegaConf.create(
    {"slow_computation": "${hya.pow:2,1000}", "fast_value": 42}  # Not computed yet
)

# Only computed when accessed
result = conf.slow_computation  # Computed here

OmegaConf does not cache the output of a resolver: every access of an interpolation calls the resolver again, even when several keys point to the same interpolation. Compute an expensive value once in Python and store it in the configuration if it is used many times:

model:
  vocab_size: 50000
  embedding_dim: 512
  total_embeddings: ${hya.mul:${model.vocab_size},${model.embedding_dim}}

layer1:
  input_size: ${model.total_embeddings} # Calls hya.mul at each access

layer2:
  input_size: ${model.total_embeddings} # Calls hya.mul at each access

docs.title: Resolver Not Found
docs.text:
Error: omegaconf.errors.UnsupportedInterpolationType: Unsupported interpolation type hya.xxx

Solution: Make sure you have imported hya:

import hya  # This line is required!
from omegaconf import OmegaConf

docs.title: Optional Dependency Missing
docs.text:
Error: omegaconf.errors.UnsupportedInterpolationType: Unsupported interpolation type hya.braceexpand

The optional resolvers (hya.braceexpand, hya.np.array, hya.torch.*) are registered only if their package is installed. Calling the resolver function directly without the package raises RuntimeError: 'braceexpand' package is required but not installed.

Solution: Install the required package:

pip install braceexpand  # or numpy, or torch

docs.title: Resolver Already Registered
docs.text:
Error: RuntimeError: A resolver is already registered for 'my_key'

Solution: Use exist_ok=True to override the resolver of the registry:

@registry.register("my_key", exist_ok=True)
def my_resolver(x):
    return x

Warning: A resolver is already registered in OmegaConf for 'my_key': not replaced.

OmegaConf already has a resolver for this key and register_resolvers() did not replace it.

Solution: Use registry.register_resolvers(replace=True) to replace it.

docs.title: Type Errors in Resolvers
docs.text:
Error: TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'

Solution: Ensure your configuration passes correct types:

# Wrong: Mixing types
result: ${hya.add:5,abc}

# Correct: Same types
result: ${hya.add:5,10}

docs.title: Circular References
docs.text:
Error: omegaconf.errors.InterpolationResolutionError: Circular reference detected

Solution: Avoid self-referential configurations:

# Wrong: Circular reference
x: ${hya.add:${y},1}
y: ${hya.add:${x},1}

# Correct: No circular dependency
x: 5
y: ${hya.add:${x},1}

docs.title: Working with Complex Data Types
docs.text:
Create NumPy arrays and PyTorch tensors:

import hya
from omegaconf import OmegaConf

conf = OmegaConf.create(
    {
        "numpy_array": "${hya.np.array:[[1,2,3],[4,5,6]]}",
        "torch_tensor": "${hya.torch.tensor:[1.0,2.0,3.0]}",
        "torch_dtype": "${hya.torch.dtype:float32}",
    }
)

print(type(conf.numpy_array))  # <class 'numpy.ndarray'>
print(type(conf.torch_tensor))  # <class 'torch.Tensor'>
print(conf.torch_dtype)  # torch.float32

docs.title: Combining Multiple Resolvers
docs.text:
Chain resolvers for complex operations:

model:
  base_size: 64
  multiplier: 4
  layers: 3

  # Compute total size: (64 * 4) * 3 = 768
  intermediate_size: ${hya.mul:${model.base_size},${model.multiplier}}
  total_size: ${hya.mul:${model.intermediate_size},${model.layers}}

docs.title: Using Resolvers with OmegaConf Features
docs.text:
Combine resolvers with OmegaConf's native features:

defaults:
  - base_config

# Use resolvers with variable interpolation
paths:
  root: /data
  project: ${oc.env:PROJECT_NAME,default_project}
  output: ${hya.iter_join:[${paths.root},${paths.project}],/}

# Use resolvers with optional values
model:
  size: ${size:512} # Can be overridden via command line
  doubled_size: ${hya.mul:${model.size},2}

docs.text:
Implement a resolver registry.

This class manages a collection of resolver functions that can be registered with keys and later used with OmegaConf.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default state Mapping[str, Callable[..., Any]] | None

Optional initial state mapping containing key-resolver pairs. If provided, a copy is made to prevent external modifications.

None Example 
>>> from hya.registry import ResolverRegistry
>>> registry = ResolverRegistry()
>>> @registry.register("my_key")
... def my_resolver(value):
...     pass
...

has_resolver(key: str) -> bool

Check if a resolver is explicitly registered for the given key.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default key str

The key to check.

required

Type Description bool

True if a resolver is registered for this key,

bool

False otherwise

docs.title: hya.ResolverRegistry.register
docs.text:
register(
    key: str, *, exist_ok: bool = False
) -> Callable[[F], F]

Register a resolver to registry with the specified key.

This method returns a decorator that can be used to register resolver functions.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default key str

The key used to register the resolver. Must be unique unless exist_ok is True.

required exist_ok bool

If False, a RuntimeError is raised if you try to register a new resolver with an existing key. If True, the existing resolver will be overridden.

False

Returns:

Type Description Callable[[F], F]

A decorator function that registers the resolver and returns it unchanged.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

If the resolver is not callable.

RuntimeError

If the key already exists and exist_ok is False.

Example 
>>> from hya.registry import ResolverRegistry
>>> registry = ResolverRegistry()
>>> @registry.register("my_key")
... def my_resolver(value):
...     return value * 2
...
>>> my_resolver(5)
10

docs.title: hya.ResolverRegistry.register_lazy
docs.text:
register_lazy(
    key: str, target: str, *, exist_ok: bool = False
) -> None

Register a resolver that is imported on its first call.

The module of the resolver is not imported when the resolver is registered, but the first time OmegaConf calls the resolver. It is useful for the resolvers that need a heavy package, because the package is not imported if the resolver is never used.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default key str

The key used to register the resolver. Must be unique unless exist_ok is True.

required target str

The resolver to import, as "module:function", for example "hya.numpy:to_array_resolver".

required exist_ok bool

If False, a RuntimeError is raised if you try to register a new resolver with an existing key. If True, the existing resolver will be overridden.

False

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If target is not formatted as "module:function".

RuntimeError

If the key already exists and exist_ok is False.

Example 
>>> from hya.registry import ResolverRegistry
>>> registry = ResolverRegistry()
>>> registry.register_lazy("hya.np.array", "hya.numpy:to_array_resolver")
>>> registry.has_resolver("hya.np.array")
True

docs.title: hya.ResolverRegistry.register_resolvers
docs.text:
register_resolvers(*, replace: bool = False) -> None

Register the resolvers to OmegaConf.

This method publishes the registered resolvers to OmegaConf. It is idempotent: a resolver already published by this registry is not registered again, so calling this method twice changes nothing. A resolver is not published, and a warning is emitted, if OmegaConf already has a resolver for its key (a resolver published before the registry changed, or registered by another source) and replace is False.

The resolvers are published with annotation_validation="off": the annotations of the resolvers are not a runtime contract.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default replace bool

If True, the resolvers replace the resolvers that OmegaConf already has for the same keys. If False, these keys are skipped with a warning.

False Notes

OmegaConf caches the resolved value of the nodes of a configuration. Replacing a resolver does not clear the cache of the existing configurations: use OmegaConf.clear_cache(cfg) to clear it.

Example 
>>> from hya.registry import ResolverRegistry
>>> registry = ResolverRegistry()
>>> @registry.register("multiply")
... def multiply_resolver(x, y):
...     return x * y
...
>>> registry.register_resolvers()

docs.title: hya.get_default_registry cached
docs.text:
get_default_registry() -> ResolverRegistry

Get or create the default global resolver registry.

Returns a singleton registry instance using a simple singleton pattern. The registry initially contains the default resolvers and can be extended with custom resolvers. The resolvers that need an optional package (braceexpand, numpy or torch) are in the registry only if the package is installed, and the module of such a resolver is imported on its first call, not when hya is imported.

This function uses a singleton pattern to ensure the same registry instance is returned on subsequent calls, which is efficient and maintains consistency across an application.

Returns:

Type Description ResolverRegistry

A ResolverRegistry instance

Notes

The singleton pattern means modifications to the returned registry affect all future calls to this function. If you need an isolated registry, create a new ResolverRegistry instance directly.

Example 
>>> from hya import get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> @registry.register("my_key")
... def my_resolver(value):
...     pass
...

add_resolver(first: Any, *others: Any) -> Any

Return the addition of several objects.

The arguments are not modified: first is never extended in place, so interpolating a list of the configuration does not change it.

docs.text:
ceildiv_resolver(dividend: float, divisor: float) -> float

Compute the ceiling division of two numbers.

Ceiling division rounds the result up to the nearest integer, which is useful for calculating the minimum number of chunks needed to accommodate a given total.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default dividend float

The dividend (numerator).

required divisor float

The divisor (denominator).

required

The ceiling of dividend / divisor. Equivalent to

Convert all items in an iterable to strings and join them.

This resolver takes an iterable (e.g., list, tuple) and concatenates all elements into a single string, separated by the specified separator. Each element is converted to a string using str().

docs.title: hya.resolvers.path_resolver
docs.text:
path_resolver(path: str) -> Path

Return a resolved path object from a string path or a file URL.

This resolver converts a string to a pathlib.Path object: it expands the user home directory (~) and resolves the path to an absolute path. A string that starts with file: is read as a file URL: the path of the URL is used, with its percent-encoding (for example %20 for a space) decoded. Any other string is a plain path, written as is: ? and % are not interpreted.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default path str

The target path as a string, or a file: URL.

required

Returns:

Type Description Path

A fully resolved pathlib.Path object with expanded user

Path

directory and converted to absolute path.

Note

Within an OmegaConf interpolation, a path with a tilde (~) must be quoted (${hya.path:"~/data"}); unquoted, the interpolation is a grammar error.

Example 
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> import hya
>>> from omegaconf import OmegaConf
>>> conf = OmegaConf.create({"key": "${hya.path:/my/path}"})
>>> conf.key
PosixPath('/my/path')
>>> conf = OmegaConf.create({"key": "${hya.path:file:///my/path%20to}"})
>>> conf.key
PosixPath('/my/path to')
>>> conf = OmegaConf.create({"key": '${hya.path:"~/my/path"}'})
>>> conf.key == Path("~/my/path").expanduser().resolve()
True

docs.title: hya.braceexpand
docs.text:
Implement a braceexpand resolver for brace expansion patterns.

This module provides OmegaConf resolvers that use the braceexpand library to expand string patterns with brace notation (similar to bash brace expansion). The resolver is registered only if the braceexpand package is available.

docs.title: hya.braceexpand.braceexpand_resolver
docs.text:
braceexpand_resolver(pattern: str) -> list[str]

Return the list of the strings of a brace expansion of pattern.

This resolver expands a string with brace patterns similar to bash brace expansion, generating multiple strings from a single pattern. Useful for generating lists of similar configuration values.

Please check https://github.com/trendels/braceexpand for more information about the syntax.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default pattern str

Specifies the pattern of the brace expansion. Supports numeric ranges (e.g., "file{1..3}.txt"), character sequences (e.g., "{a,b,c}"), and nested patterns.

required

Returns:

Type Description list[str]

The list of the strings resulting from the brace expansion of

list[str]

the pattern. It is a list (and not an iterator), so it has a

list[str]

length, can be indexed and can be read several times. The

list[str]

whole expansion is built at once.

Note

When using brace expansion patterns in OmegaConf, you need to quote the pattern string (${hya.braceexpand:"a{1,2}"}) or to escape the braces to avoid conflicts with OmegaConf's own syntax for curly braces.

Example 
>>> import hya
>>> from omegaconf import OmegaConf
>>> conf = OmegaConf.create({"key": '${hya.braceexpand:"file_{1..3}.txt"}'})
>>> list(conf.key)
['file_1.txt', 'file_2.txt', 'file_3.txt']
>>> len(conf.key)
3

docs.title: hya.numpy
docs.text:
Implement NumPy resolvers for array creation and manipulation.

This module provides OmegaConf resolvers that use NumPy for array operations. The resolvers are registered only if the numpy package is available, allowing users to create NumPy arrays directly from configuration files. registry.register_resolvers()

docs.title: Then in your OmegaConf config: # data: ${hya.np.array:[1, 2, 3]}
hya.numpy.to_array_resolver
docs.text:
to_array_resolver(data: ArrayLike) -> ndarray

Implement a resolver to transform the input to a numpy.ndarray.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data ArrayLike

Specifies the data to transform in numpy.ndarray. This value should be compatible with numpy.array

required

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

The input in a numpy.ndarray object.

Example 
>>> import hya
>>> from omegaconf import OmegaConf
>>> conf = OmegaConf.create({"key": "${hya.np.array:[1, 2, 3]}"})
>>> conf.key
array([1, 2, 3])

docs.title: hya.torch
docs.text:
Implement PyTorch resolvers for tensor creation and dtype handling.

This module provides OmegaConf resolvers that use PyTorch for tensor operations and data type specifications. The resolvers are registered only if the torch package is available, enabling users to create PyTorch tensors and specify dtypes directly from configuration files.

docs.title: hya.torch.to_tensor_resolver
docs.text:
to_tensor_resolver(data: Any) -> Tensor

Implement a resolver to transform the input to a torch.Tensor.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data Any

Specifies the data to transform in torch.Tensor. This value should be compatible with torch.tensor

required

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

The input in a torch.Tensor object.

Example 
>>> import hya
>>> from omegaconf import OmegaConf
>>> conf = OmegaConf.create({"key": "${hya.torch.tensor:[1,2,3,4,5]}"})
>>> conf.key
tensor([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

docs.title: hya.torch.torch_dtype_resolver
docs.text:
torch_dtype_resolver(target: str) -> dtype

Create a torch.dtype from its string representation.

This resolver converts a string name to the corresponding PyTorch data type object. The string must match an attribute name in the torch module that represents a dtype (e.g., "float32", "int64").

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default target str

The target data type as a string. Must be a valid torch dtype attribute name such as "float", "float32", "float64", "int32", "int64", "bool", etc. The string should match the attribute name in torch (e.g., use "float32" not "torch.float32").

required

Returns:

Type Description dtype

The corresponding torch.dtype object.

Raises:

Type Description InterpolationResolutionError

If the target string doesn't correspond to a valid torch dtype. The message lists the available dtype names, sorted.

Example 
>>> import hya
>>> from omegaconf import OmegaConf
>>> conf = OmegaConf.create({"key": "${hya.torch.dtype:float}"})
>>> conf.key
torch.float32
>>> conf = OmegaConf.create({"key": "${hya.torch.dtype:int64}"})
>>> conf.key
torch.int64
